name: Sewer socialism
summary: Sewer socialism was the Milwaukee Social-Democrats' reformist, municipal socialism from the 1890s to 1960. It aimed at winning city hall and showing that honest, efficient public enterprise (water, sewage, power, parks, schools, housing) improves workers' lives, while building union strength and working toward a planned economy of publicly owned industries by ballots, not violent revolution. Its leaders Victor Berger, Emil Seidel and Daniel Hoan attacked revolutionary phrases and sectarian rules, opposed the First World War, and worked inside the AFL unions.
scope: The Milwaukee Social-Democratic movement named 'sewer socialism' by the sources (the Wisconsin Historical Society, Blanc, PBS Wisconsin, WUWM, JSTOR Daily), as represented by its three leaders Victor Berger, Emil Seidel and Daniel Hoan, with Berger's 1906 and 1921 writings and the party's record in Milwaukee city government and the Wisconsin legislature. It excludes the later Zeidler-era liberalism, modern revivals such as 'pothole politics', and the broader democratic socialism or the national Socialist Party, audited separately.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Hoan reformed the police with a merit system, higher pay and training, and the Socialists pushed for better wages for police; Milwaukee never considered defunding them.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Milwaukee's Socialists met poverty and recreation needs with public programmes: parks, playgrounds, social centres and material relief.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Berger said the Socialist Party took a stand against inherited prejudices about imperialism, which covers one society ruling another to improve it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Berger wrote in 1911 that the distinguishing trait of Socialists is that they understand the class struggle, and the party framed nearly all its agitation as workers against capitalists.

collective-bargaining.rationale: In 1935 the Social-Democrats passed the Boncel Ordinance, which let the city close plants that refused to bargain collectively.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Berger said the Socialist Party took a stand against the inherited prejudices about the value of commercialism, patriotism and imperialism.

corporate-influence.rationale: Berger called the US government one of the plutocracy and capitalist class, and the Socialists ran Milwaukee on ending the sway of monied interests and monopolies in city government.

democracy-best.rationale: Berger wrote that 'all politics is compromise, because it means abiding by the will of the majority', even though the Socialists did not have the majority.

direct-action.rationale: The Social-Democrats built their strategy on electoral campaigns and fights for policy changes, and fought the Wobblies' competing industrial unions.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Berger condemned the wartime government's suppression of Socialists as tyranny and was proud of the party's record in resisting it.

gradual-change.rationale: Berger endorsed 'a policy of steady change' and reforms 'one step, two steps, or six steps at a time', and said there are no sudden leaps in history.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The Socialists held that utilities and basic services such as water, sewage, power, lighting and parks should be controlled by the public, and they municipalised several of them.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Wisconsin Historical Society says Milwaukee Socialists sought to replace the capitalist system with a planned economy of state-owned industries.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The Social-Democrats sought to end private contracts for all utilities and replace them with city operation, succeeding for several.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Socialist city governments ran a quarry, a power plant, cooperative housing and Mayor Hoan's public food sales alongside the city's private firms.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Socialist city governments took on health inspection, vaccination, zoning, housing, parks, social centres and utilities.

no-business-privileges.rationale: As city attorney Hoan fought the utility and street-railway companies for lower fees and better service.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Socialists governed Milwaukee as one party among others, and Mayor Hoan left office after losing the 1940 election.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: The Wisconsin Historical Society records that Milwaukee Socialists did not advocate violent revolution: socialism was to come by ballots.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Berger said in 1921 that all other parties or groups, however progressive, were always uncertain and often dishonest, in contrast to the Socialists.

production-for-use.rationale: Hoan sold surplus Army food and clothing through city offices at well below retail prices and presented it as showing that enterprises can run without profit.

property-fundamental.rationale: The city used condemnation to get land for parks, sewage works and harbour, including the eviction of the Jones Island residents, over their court challenge.

public-ownership.rationale: Milwaukee's Socialist administrations built a city-owned power plant and municipalised the quarry, street lighting, sewage disposal and water purification, and tried and failed to bring the electric and street-railway utilities under city ownership.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: In Congress Berger fought immigration restrictions, according to Blanc.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In Congress Berger fought immigration restrictions, according to Blanc.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Socialist administrations backed striking workers; Mayor Seidel threatened to swear in strikers as police deputies, and the city's labour law punished employers who refused to bargain.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Berger asked for concrete political achievements over theoretical treatises, and the party built its tactics on analysis of public opinion rather than imported formulas.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Berger wanted a systematic way of arming all the people, saying an armed people is always free.

state-harmful.rationale: The Socialists built their programme on winning and running city government and expanding its services.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hoan spoke out strongly against the idea that lower taxes were needed and argued for a fairer tax structure that paid for services.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Berger said the Socialist Party took a stand against inherited prejudices about imperialism, which covers expansion by a strong nation.

unions-good.rationale: Socialist administrations did everything possible to boost union power, using union labour on city work and backing unionisation drives among city workers.

war-builds-character.rationale: Berger called the World War the greatest triumph of darkness and reaction in a thousand years and said it revived national prejudices and race hatreds.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Berger said the United States had a government of the plutocracy and the capitalist class that suppressed Socialistic and liberal ideas.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: Berger called a class alliance with farmers of progressive views a prerequisite without which there is no chance for Socialism, and in 1921 wanted a big party based on trade unions, farmers and sympathetic intellectuals.

workers-councils.rationale: The Socialists pursued power through elected seats, passing 295 bills in the Wisconsin legislature in 1919-1931 and sending Berger to Congress, not through councils.

workers-own-party.rationale: Milwaukee's Socialists founded their own Social-Democratic Party in 1897 and guarded its autonomy against the national party and other parties for decades.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: After 1904 the Social-Democrats put immediate reform demands at the centre of their election campaigns and fought to pass them in office.

notes: Researched themes: economy and public ownership (WHS, Blanc, WUWM, Hoan's record), unions and the party (Blanc, Berger), government and tactics (Berger 1906 and 1921), war and empire (Berger 1921), policing and taxes (Hoan). Sources are mostly secondary accounts of the Milwaukee record; the many statements the sources never address stay null. Further themes searched in the saved sources for the widest lines (religion and church, race, lynching and the Klan, patriotism and the flag, nationalism) found only Berger's 1921 stand against 'commercialism, patriotism, imperialism' and his fight against lynching and immigration restrictions, and no stated position on the statements of those lines. Earlier answers that were inferred from general aims were nulled with a reviewHistory entry.
